analysis.title: Commodity Comment: Pressure Builds
key_insights: RBC sees the direction of travel in the Middle East pointing to near-term escalation, despite another round of anonymous media reports from Pakistani and Qatari officials on deal progress. The reports came as Brent breached $110/bbl.

RBC sees little incentive for Iran to ease its pressure campaign with the US midterms less than two weeks away. Tehran's leverage looks higher with the Houthis continuing to attack critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

Attacks on tankers and maritime traffic have worsened in recent weeks despite elevated Gulf loadings and exports. There were at least 16 attacks on ships last week, including two sunk Emirati-linked cargo ships. RBC says an increasing number of attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz are going unreported.

A Houthi attack on an Aramco field in eastern Saudi Arabia was intercepted on Wednesday and resulted in two fatalities. Riyadh Airport remains effectively closed, and RBC is watching reports that the US is withdrawing non-essential diplomatic staff from Saudi posts.

RBC treats rising crude exports through the Strait as a lagging indicator of regional pressure. It points to the large financial and military cost of the US-led escort operation. It expects more congressional scrutiny of that cost if Democrats win one or both chambers.
Dated Brent is around $119.79/bbl, up m/m but slightly off recent highs. The term portion of the Brent curve has also rerated higher, reflecting a tighter-for-longer view.

Middle East volumes have been elevated for several weeks but may be about to slow. RBC's data show 7-day moving average commodity transits in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday were 4 vessels lower w/w (about 15% lower), and this week's transits look set to fall further. Recent strikes could be deterring operators or threatening the ship-to-ship transfer system.

Natural gas prices fell this week to multiweek lows as production recovered and NOAA outlooks favored above-normal temperatures across much of the northern and eastern US, which reduces expected heating demand.

LNG feedgas demand topped 21 bcf/d this week, a new high, as maintenance season ended. Golden Pass Train 1 topped 800 MMcf/d of feedgas demand ahead of commercial operations in Q4. Trains 2 and 3 could add another 1.6-1.7 Bcf/d through 2027. RBC calls this a growing structural counterweight to seasonal weakness, but near-term direction depends on temperatures and the pace of production recovery.

Central bank buying is a key pillar of RBC's constructive secular view on gold, which expects ongoing net purchases. Russia sold about 6.2t in September, its 10th straight month of sales, taking holdings to the lowest since 2019.

IMF data show about 337t of net central bank gold purchases in 2026 through August. World Gold Council data, which count unreported official-sector activity, put H1 2026 at 345.4t. China added about 23t in September, extending its buying streak to 23 months. Poland and central Asian countries are also among top buyers. RBC cites de-dollarization, diversification and geopolitics as drivers.

The US ITC ruled last week that imports from India, Indonesia and Laos injured US solar manufacturers, clearing the way for more AD/CVD duties. African nations now account for 40% of solar module imports in 2026, led by Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and Djibouti.

Commerce's July anti-circumvention investigation into Ethiopia examines whether Chinese components processed there are evading duties. Chinese cell shipments to Ethiopia have collapsed while Kenya and Nigeria keep absorbing supply, raising the prospect of broader investigations into Chinese-linked manufacturing in Africa. A preliminary ruling is expected in December and a final decision in May.

CFTC data as of 13-Oct-26 show gold managed money at 27.0% net long of futures open interest (28.0% a week earlier) and swap dealers at -56.5% net. Natural gas managed money is -7.3% net, Nymex crude is +2.1% and palladium is -46.2%.

Mild winter forecasts weigh on prices, while record LNG feedgas demand gives structural support.

risk_factors: Further escalation around the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on vessels, many of which go unreported.
Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and the possibility that attacks hinder Middle East loadings.
A slowdown in Strait transits, which RBC's latest data hint at.
Mild winter weather and recovering production pushing natural gas lower.
Russian gold selling offsetting central bank buying elsewhere.
AD/CVD duties and anti-circumvention investigations disrupting solar supply chains.
vol_and_positioning: Gold managed money net long was 27.0% of futures open interest as of 13-Oct-26, versus 28.0% a week earlier. Gold swap dealers were -56.5% net.
Natural gas managed money was -7.3% net long of open interest (-8.0% a week earlier). Nymex crude was +2.1% and ICE crude -0.7%.
Palladium managed money was -46.2% net and lumber -58.7%. Soybean meal (31.8%), gasoline (28.8%) and oats (28.5%) were the most net long.
Total managed money across major commodity futures was 6.1% net long of open interest, versus 6.8% a week earlier.

tension_points.bull_case: Anonymous Pakistani and Qatari officials report progress toward a deal, and Gulf loadings and exports have risen in recent weeks.
tension_points.bear_case: RBC sees little incentive for Iran to ease pressure before the midterms. Attacks on ships are rising, Houthis are hitting Saudi infrastructure, and rising exports are a lagging indicator.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A verified deal or sustained de-escalation, which would undercut RBC's escalation call.
